title: History of Abu Niyyah and Abu Niyyatayn

keywords: history of abu niyyah and abu niyyatayn
full_text:
Two traveling companions journeyed across the desert of Nejd: Abu Niyyah (He of Good Faith), whose heart was simple, honest, and trusting, and Abu Niyyatayn (He of Two Intentions), who was scheming, jealous, and deceitful.

As their water ran dry beneath the blazing sun, Abu Niyyah shared his remaining drops with his companion. But when Abu Niyyah's canteen was empty, Abu Niyyatayn refused to share a single sip of his water unless Abu Niyyah surrendered all his gold and even his woolen cloak!
Having taken everything, the treacherous Abu Niyyatayn abandoned his companion half-dead beside a desolate dry well, riding away on the camel.

Abu Niyyah dragged himself into the shade of the well's stone wall, whispering prayers of patience and forgiveness.
As night fell, two desert spirits alighted upon the rim of the well. Believing themselves alone, one spirit said to the other:
'Dost thou know that the King of Damascus suffers from an incurable blindness, which no royal physician can heal? Yet the cure is simple: three drops of dew from the leaves of the wild jujube bush growing behind this well, dropped into his eyes at sunrise, will restore his sight instantly!'
The second spirit added: 'And dost thou know that beneath the dry foundation of this very well lies a buried chest containing the lost emerald signet of King Solomon, alongside an abundant spring of sweet water that would turn this entire wilderness into a blossoming garden?'

When dawn broke, Abu Niyyah gathered the dew from the jujube leaves, drank from the moisture, and dug beneath the well stone. Instantly, sweet water gushed forth, accompanied by the ancient signet ring!

Abu Niyyah traveled to Damascus, requested an audience with the blind King, and applied the jujube dew to the monarch's eyes.
Instantly, the King's blindness was dissolved! Overjoyed, the King made Abu Niyyah his Grand Vizier and gave him the royal princess in marriage.

Years later, a ragged, miserable beggar was brought to the vizier's diwan: it was Abu Niyyatayn, who had lost his ill-gotten wealth to bandits and lived in squalor.
Instead of taking revenge, the noble Abu Niyyah embraced him, fed him, and gave him a purse of gold, saying:
'Brother, I harbor no malice. Good faith has brought me honor, while two intentions brought thee misery.'

Envious to the core, Abu Niyyatayn asked how Abu Niyyah had gained his fortune. Abu Niyyah honestly recounted the story of the desert well and the spirits.
Greedy Abu Niyyatayn immediately rode to the same well, hid beneath the stone wall, and waited for the spirits to arrive, hoping to overhear more secrets.

At midnight, the spirits returned, furious:
'Someone has revealed our secrets! The King's sight is healed, the water flows, and the emerald signet is gone! A spy must be lurking near!'
Searching the shadows, the spirits found Abu Niyyatayn cowering behind the stones and hurled him into the bottomless pit, where his treachery was buried forever.

Abu Niyyah governed Damascus with righteousness and peace, proving that sincere goodness is an impenetrable fortress against evil.
moral: A pure intention brings divine protection and eventual glory, while malice and double-minded deceit destroy their own author.
